extracted.intended_audience: jurors in U.S. federal patent infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model/bench jury instructions explaining what a patent is, how claims define coverage, standards for infringement and invalidity, burden/standards of proof, and related legal concepts jurors must apply in a U.S. patent trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of a U.S. patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid United States patent gives the patent holder the right [for up to 20 years from the date the patent application was filed] [for 17 years from the date the patent issued] to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the patented invention within the United States, or from importing it into the United States, without the patent holder’s permission. A violation of the patent holder’s rights is called infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the basic legal entitlement that the jury is adjudicating; infringement is enforcement of these rights by lawsuit in federal court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and claims as components of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application includes a 'specification' containing a written description of the claimed invention telling what the invention is, how it works, how to make it, and how to use it. The specification concludes with one or more numbered sentences called the patent 'claims.' When the patent is granted, the claims define the boundaries of its protection and give notice to the public of those boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The figures and text provide context and examples, but it is the claims that define the breadth of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prosecution and prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of obtaining a patent (patent prosecution) involves filing an application with the PTO and interaction with Examiners; the written communications between the Examiner and the applicant are the 'prosecution history.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history may bear on claim meaning or other issues; the Examiner issues Office Actions and the applicant may amend claims or respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art and its use in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO searches for and reviews information that is publicly available or submitted by the applicant called 'prior art.' The Examiner reviews prior art to determine whether the invention is truly an advance over the state of the art at the time the application was filed. A patent lists the prior art the Examiner considered (the 'cited references').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art generally includes information demonstrating the state of technology that existed before the claimed invention was made or before the application was filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of infringement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be infringed by making, using, selling, or offering for sale in the United States, or by importing into the United States, a product or by using a method meeting all the requirements of a claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim; there may be infringement as to one claim but not another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement: inducement and contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] may also indirectly infringe the patent by contributing to infringement by another entity, or by inducing another person or entity to infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate instructions (provided elsewhere) will explain the requirements for contributory and induced infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding infringement and invalidity, issues are assessed on a claim-by-claim basis; each claim is effectively treated as if it were a separate patent and may cover more or less than another claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must determine what each claim covers and then apply infringement/invalidity analyses to each asserted claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge’s role in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge's role to define the terms of the claims, and it is the jury's role to apply those definitions to the issues in the case. The jury must accept the court's definitions of claim terms provided to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the court has provided claim constructions or a glossary, the jury is to apply those definitions throughout the case; the judge's constructions are not an indication of views on infringement or validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: How a claim defines what it covers (claim elements/limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim sets forth, in words, a set of requirements (claim elements or limitations) in a single sentence. If a device or method satisfies each of these requirements, then it is covered by the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a thing meets all the claim elements, the claim 'covers' that thing. Understanding claim language is necessary to decide infringement and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim sets forth all requirements that must be met to be covered by that claim. A dependent claim refers to another claim for some requirements, incorporates all requirements of the claim(s) to which it refers, and adds its own additional requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine what a dependent claim covers, look at both the dependent claim and any claim(s) to which it refers. It may be helpful to submit a chart showing dependencies for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional claim language: 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructions explain how transitional phrases affect claim scope: e.g., 'comprising' is open-ended and allows additional undisclosed elements; 'consisting of' is closed and means 'I claim what follows and nothing else'; 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate in scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites authorities (cases) illustrating these meanings and their practical effect on claim breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is not new (is anticipated) if all of the elements of the claim are present in a single previous device or method, or sufficiently described in a single previous printed publication or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation must be proven by clear and convincing evidence (see burden of proof entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be invalid as obvious even if every element is not shown in a single piece of prior art; it is invalid if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury will consider a number of questions (to be instructed later) in deciding whether claimed inventions are obvious; invalidity by obviousness must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be valid, the description of the invention in the specification must be detailed enough to demonstrate that the applicant actually possessed the invention as broadly as claimed in the claims of the issued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a separate validity inquiry from enablement; note references to appellate review (e.g., Ariad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure in the patent must be sufficiently full and clear to have allowed persons of ordinary skill in the field to make and use the invention without undue experimentation at the time the patent application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of enablement is a basis for invalidity; jury will be instructed on how to assess this when raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of proof (burden of persuasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two standards of proof: preponderance of the evidence and clear and convincing evidence. Preponderance means more likely true than not. Clear and convincing means you have been left with a clear conviction that the fact has been proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement is typically proved by a preponderance of the evidence; invalidity (and certain other defenses) must be proved by clear and convincing evidence. The instruction explains clear and convincing lies between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages principles and reasonable royalty floor
rubrics_metrics.description: If you decide any claim has been infringed and is not invalid, you must decide money damages to compensate the patent holder and put it in approximately the same financial position it would have been in had the infringement not occurred; damages may not be punitive and must be at least what the patent holder would have received as a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willfulness is a separate finding that the court will consider later and should not directly increase the compensatory damages awarded by the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity/unenforceability proof allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused infringer must persuade the jury by clear and convincing evidence that a claim is invalid (and/or unenforceable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accused infringer will present evidence of invalidity and may rebut the patent holder's proofs; the sequence of presentation (opening, evidence, rebuttal, closings) is described in the trial outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation evidence types
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation can be shown by a single previous device or method, or a single previous printed publication or patent that sufficiently describes all claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies what qualifies as prior art for anticipation purposes; the Examiner's cited references are examples of prior art considered during prosecution.
